However, as investors revised their outlook to see the Fed staying patient, the dollar retreated from its peak.
In the New York close, the dollar index (DXY), which tracks the greenback against six major currencies, rose 0.34% to 102.53, after having briefly climbed to 102.94 earlier in the session.
Data released by the U.S. Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics showed that September’s consumer price index rose sharply, driven by a large jump in gasoline prices.
State Street senior global markets strategist Marvin Loh said, “CPI data is still influencing market valuations, and the stock market decline provides another reason to push the dollar higher.”

The inflation report eclipsed recent dovish signals from Fed officials, including comments from New York Fed President John Williams, whose remarks had weakened the dollar on the previous trading day.
Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman also signaled on Thursday that the central bank would adopt a wait‑and‑see stance before any further rate hikes.
Meanwhile, the Fed’s Beige Book released on Wednesday showed that the U.S. labor market remains in a “low‑hiring, low‑layoff” environment, though inflation pressures have risen in some regions.

Mesirow Currency Management senior investment strategist Uto Shinohara said, “The Fed’s dual mandate is still at odds with signs of a weakening labor market. Tomorrow’s retail sales, initial jobless claims and producer price index (PPI) data should give us a clearer picture of consumer conditions, the labor market and price pressures.”

CME Group’s FedWatch tool shows traders now assign a 65% probability that the Fed will keep rates unchanged at its Oct. 27‑28 meeting, up from 53% a month ago. The market expects a cumulative tightening of about 79 basis points by the end of 2027.
The U.S. central bank raised its policy rate by 0.25 percentage point last month, moving the target range to 3.75%‑4.00%.
Angeles Investments chief investment officer Michael Rosen said investors are losing confidence that the United States will take decisive action to curb inflation.

Rosen added, “We see the dollar’s strength being supported by higher rates. Unless the Fed hikes aggressively enough to push the economy into recession, or we overhaul trade and immigration policy, inflation won’t come down.”

Finance and central‑bank leaders from multiple countries are gathered in Bangkok for the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.

IMF finance chief Rodrigo Valdes said the Fund has stepped up its calls for governments to rein in soaring debt. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva added that the United States needs fiscal adjustments to put its debt on a more sustainable path.

French sovereign bonds have been among the hardest hit in the recent global bond sell‑off. Investors worry that political battles ahead of next year’s presidential election could hamper France’s efforts to reduce its large fiscal deficit.

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde, speaking at a CNN event in Bangkok, said France should address its debt problem through fiscal consolidation. Her remarks dampened market speculation that the ECB might start buying French bonds to lower yields.
Higher oil prices and continued concerns about France’s fiscal health have added further pressure on the euro.
The euro fell 0.41% to $1.1152, hitting a 17‑month low against the dollar and a 16‑month low against the pound.

UniCredit foreign‑exchange strategist Roberto Mialich said the euro could test $1.10 in the short term, but he is less pessimistic about its trajectory by year‑end, expecting “U.S. Treasury yields may retreat even though euro‑area conditions could still weigh on the euro.”

The Financial Times reported on Wednesday that UK Treasury Secretary John Healey expects all new spending announced in this month’s budget to be funded by tax hikes or cuts rather than additional borrowing.
An IMF senior official said the institution has not advised the United Kingdom to accelerate its fiscal consolidation pace.
The pound slipped 0.59% to $1.3177.
The dollar fell 0.08% against the yen, to ¥158.16.
